children.translated_text: One should not fear, nor understand,
nor listen to the opponent's words;
one should retort instantly—
[this is the way] for those who wish to triumph in assemblies.
Composure, shamelessness,
contempt for the opponent,
laughter, praise of the king—and thus
these five are the causes of victory.
One should win by shouting loudly
if the judge is unlearned;
if he is learned, then right there
partiality should be imposed upon him.
Greed is the reason, wealth is the goal,
the family priest is the illustration,
self-aggrandizement is the conclusion—
this is the method in inferences.
Truth must be practiced with shame
by one who seeks knowledge for a long time;
by one who seeks victory, modesty should be abandoned,
and a great uproar should be made.
Through lectures and the composition of treatises,
renown is obtained for a while;
and whether genuine learning [comes] thus
at the end of one's life or not.
Who on the face of the earth will be
the praisers of a fool?

children.text: na stauti cet svayaṃ ca svaṃ
children.translated_text: If he does not praise himself,
when will he ever find satisfaction?

children.text: na stauti cet svayaṃ ca svaṃ

children.translated_text: "The time for discussion has passed;
it will become clear later"—
for those who teach thus from texts,
where is the difficulty?
Helplessness, excessive faith,
and satisfaction with a semblance of knowledge—
these three qualities of a student
are born from the fortune of a foolish teacher.
If the mind does not advance at all
in any branch of learning,
'We shall become <s>māntrikas</s> (sorcerers),
or <s>yogins</s>, or ascetics.'
Without delay in [achieving] success,
<s>māntrikas</s> (sorcerers) obtain fame;
if there is delay, abundance of ritual work
is proclaimed, and wealth is obtained.
Happiness among the happy, and a livelihood
even in the misery of the miserable—
those for whom [everything] becomes a favor,
those blessed ones are truly <s>māntrikas</s>.
As long as silence [comes] from ignorance
or conduct is peculiar,
so long it culminates in the form
of greatness for the sorcerer.
Having examined the planetary movements, astrologers
should pronounce the fate of kings;
for knowledge of planetary motions
is essential for them.
'A son' if asked by the father,
'a daughter' if asked by the mother—
the astrologer who says thus in questions about pregnancy
shall be victorious.
In questions about longevity, a long life
should be predicted by the astrologers;
the living will hold [them] in high regard—
and who, after dying, will question them again?
Everything should be stated with two possibilities,
everything within two time limits,
everything as if mixed—
thus should diviners speak.
Promising wealth to the poor,
and greater wealth to the wealthy—
speaking thus, astrologers
are accepted by people in all cases.
A betel leaf for [predicting] the gain of a hundred,
a meal for a thousand—
the reproach of astrologers
is constant when events go awry.
Even the earth bounded by oceans
must be searched through,
for there is no place, even of a cubit's measure,
devoid of an astrologer.

children.text: vārān ke cid grahān ke cit
children.translated_text: Some know the weekdays, some the planets,
some know the constellations;
those who know all three
are <s>Vācaspati</s> (Bṛhaspati, lord of speech) himself.

children.text: vārān ke cid grahān ke cit

children.translated_text: Omen-readers, dream-interpreters,
and oracles of deities—[[these three]]
were created by nature as enemies
of the astrologers, these three.
From the healthy and the incurably ill,
there is nothing [to gain];
the timid and the chronically sick
are the causes of fortune for physicians.
Neither too much confidence should be given
nor too much fear to the patient;
from indifference, no gift [comes] at the beginning,
and from despair, none at the end either.
Medicine may be prescribed at will,
but the regimen should be declared strict;
recovery [is attributed] to the physician's greatness,
failure to the patient's non-compliance.
The etiology, the names of diseases,
what is suitable and unsuitable, and the treatment—
all this will be taught
by the women in the patient's house.
As diseases proliferate
and creatures die,
physicians gradually become expert
in the true nature of ailments.
At the beginning, to get things started;
in the middle, on the pretext of medicine;
and at the end, for gaining respect—
physicians seek to take [money].
When physicians are eager to obtain [a patient],
having finally found a sick person,
heirs sprout up [alongside],
as do astrologers and sorcerers.
At the onset of illness, kind words;
in the middle, some expenditure of money;
gradually, indifference when cured—
once bathed [in health], one does not see the physician.
Astrology, sorcery,
medicine, and the skill of flattery—
each one [suffices] for gaining wealth,
but a combination of two or three is rare.
Falsehood and flattering speech—
this is a great combination for wealth;
truth and learning—this
is the combination that causes poverty.
Timidity, lack of discipline,
wretchedness, and lack of discernment—
all these are cleansed by poets
who are slaves to the fistful [of grain] from the wealthy.
Poets, ready to praise,
do not look for a reason;
even if there is nothing to praise,
their tongue quivers [with eagerness].
Poets praise what has already been praised,
not discerning qualities on their own;
there is a certain insect called a bee—
how much description [can be given] of that?
A single poem of a man
serves for a village, for a horse, for an elephant,
and ultimately for food, for garments,
and for betel.
The supreme <s>Brahman</s> called 'word,'
refined through composition,
is sold by some
and wasted in vain by others.
Those people who, even having obtained <s>Vāṇī</s> (the goddess of speech), describe semblances of men—
[are like those who,]
even having obtained the wish-fulfilling cow,
yoke her to a plough.
Praising semblances of men,
prattling this way and that—
how shall poets cross over,
[they who are] speakers of the fulfillment of desires?
The mind that is absorbed
in composition, in description, in suggestion—
that is superior even to <s>samādhi</s> (deep meditation),
if <s>Śaṃkara</s> (Śiva) is the subject described.
The wife, her sister,
the parents-in-law, and the brother-in-law—
by <s>Kali</s> (the age of strife) were created for living beings
these five other vital breaths.
Sons-in-law, nephews,
maternal uncles, and the wife's relatives—
unknown to the householders,
they devour [the household] like rats in the house.
The mother is the strength of the maternal uncle,
the daughter is the strength of the son-in-law,
the wife is the strength of the father-in-law,
and the guest himself is his own strength.
The son-in-law's crookedness lasts
only as long as the brother-in-law is a child;
when he begins to awaken, simplicity [appears];
when he is fully awakened, flight.
The wife is the elder, the brother-in-law is a child,
the mother-in-law acts independently,
and the father-in-law is abroad—
such is the son-in-law's arc of fortune.
With ornaments, garments, and vessels,
and with caressing of the children—
coming just once and departing,
the daughter sweeps the house clean.
The wife calls her own relatives
eaters of dry food and sparing eaters,
but those on the husband's side, gluttons,
milk-drinkers, and even thieves.
Two wives with sons,
a sister without a husband—
'Unending Quarrel' is the name
of this combination for householders.
Two wives, many sons,
poverty, the onset of disease,
and aged mother and father—
each one is worse than hell.
At [their] mere recollection, the limbs grow feeble;
at [their] sight, reason is destroyed—
ah, how great is this specter
called the creditor!
Even <s>Antaka</s> (Death) indeed waits
for the final hour of creatures;
but no restriction of time whatsoever
exists for the creditor.
We see no fangs in his mouth,
nor a noose in his hand;
yet merely upon beholding the creditor,
the mind is nonetheless agitated.
Conciliation toward an enemy, remedy
for all diseases, meditation on <s>Mṛtyuñjaya</s> (conqueror of death) at death—
but against poverty,
there is nothing at all.
It gives strength for wandering,
it makes one endure cold and heat,
it kindles the fire in the belly—
poverty is the supreme medicine.
Speech that falters, eyes that blink,
feet that stumble—
poverty, like a king's command, drives one forward
in the act of begging.
Offenses against kings decay,
even forbidden deeds decay—
for those mighty in their utter destitution,
even stone decays in the end.
He has no thieves, no slanderers,
no heirs, no kings—
indigence is greater than kingship,
if the truth is realized.
It manifests arrogance,
it sets thieves in motion,
it encourages heirs—
<s>Lakṣmī</s> (wealth/fortune), when she arrives even slightly.
Those wealthy people who constantly
mock the learned—
they themselves are mocked
when <s>Śrī</s> (fortune) slightly neglects them.
Regarding praises as authoritative,
regarding oneself as a deity,
regarding other humans as insects—
such is the fruit of newly-arrived wealth.
Even while hearing, they ask again;
even while seeing, they do not understand—
the wealthy consider mockeries
to be nothing but praises.
Surrounding those blinded by the pride of wealth,
conspiring with one another,
the attendants laugh freely
like children, madmen, and ghosts.
They are constantly praised by those who should be praised,
and served by those who should be served—
yet the wealthy person neither fears
nor feels ashamed.
The possession by a <s>graha</s> (spirit) lasts but a moment,
the intoxication from liquor but a <s>yāma</s> (three hours)—
but the intoxication of wealth in fools
persists for the entire lifetime.
<s>Śrī</s> (fortune), having played for a month or half a month,
departs;
but the disorder once begun by her
is permanent, like the smell of garlic.
The intoxication from <s>kodrava</s> (millet) grain is in the throat,
the intoxication from betel is in the heart;
but the intoxication of wealth pervades all limbs,
even the faces of sons and wives.
Whether <s>Lakṣmī</s> was or is [present] there,
let the pride prevail there;
but how does it descend even into the family,
like leprosy or epilepsy?
They teach the <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures),
they belittle the learned,
they make one forget one's own caste—
five or six cowrie shells in the hand.
Let the rich man support his dependents
or give what is due to supplicants—
as long as [his conduct] resembles that of a beggar,
the world does not tolerate it.
The burden of other people's wealth
is indeed borne by slanderers;
how they strive to lighten it
by other means on their own!
Is the reward from kings commensurate
with the slanderer's labor?
Twofold and threefold indeed
shall <s>Kṛtānta</s> (Death/Yama) reward them.
At <s>Gokarṇa</s> and <s>Bhadrakarṇa</s>,
recitation destroys evil deeds;
in the king's ear, recitation
instantly destroys all deeds.
They desire nothing for themselves,
nor are they impelled by anyone—
they engage in others' affairs;
the wicked and the saintly are alike [in this].
A vulture perched atop a house
[portends] misfortune in time;
a rogue near the house
brings instant misfortune to living beings.
Dry fasting in religious matters,
fasting in medical matters,
and <s>japa</s>-sacrifice among sacrifices—
these please those who are covetous.
'What will he say?'—as long as the poor man
is anxious before the rich man,
'What will he ask?'—the miser too
is equally anxious about that.
The greedy put into practice
the entire meaning of the treatise on hospitality—
they who regard each morsel of begged food
as [vast as] Mount <s>Meru</s>.
The guardian of wealth, being a <s>piśāca</s> (demon), gives
when the master is present;
but the one greedy for wealth, [though also] a demon,
does not wish to give to anyone.
Givers are sought by supplicants,
and supplicants [are sought] again by givers—
from this interchange of agent and object,
oh, how great is the high and low!
'If I do not exist, there would be
no protector of the wealth'—
having thus determined, the miser
himself also somehow eats.
About to depart, [the guest] enters;
he settles in day after day;
he invents various obstacles—
[thus behaves] a guest who wishes to stay long.
One [coin] is given to a scholar,
ten to a poet, a hundred to an actor,
a thousand to a hypocrite in the world—
but to a learned <s>Vedic</s> scholar, nothing at all.
Having properly propitiated the matchmaker,
one should cultivate supreme detachment;
worldly aims succeed
as long as fickleness is concealed.
On one side, all the <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures);
on the other, a <s>tulasī</s> (holy basil) twig—
something should be said, it was declared,
but in truth, <s>tulasī</s> is supreme.
<s>Vāgbhaṭa</s> forgot this
while enumerating the virtues of <s>tulasī</s>:
'She deludes the whole world' and 'she bestows wealth'—
these two virtues.
A loincloth, an application of ashes,
a <s>darbha</s> (sacred grass) and <s>rudrākṣa</s> rosary,
silence, and eating alone—
these six are the revivers of fools.
Residence at holy <s>tīrthas</s> (pilgrimage sites),
a famous and deceased <s>guru</s>,
and teaching activities—
these should be proclaimed by seekers of wealth.
When the <s>mantra</s> is forgotten, 'it is the tradition';
when Sanskrit has lapsed, 'it is the [local] practice';
when conduct is lacking, 'it is the regional custom'—
for questioners, the answer is ready.
So that many may know,
so that [they] may speak [well] of the donor—
thus one should perform all <s>dharma</s> (religious duties);
nothing should be done in vain.
A <s>japa</s> (recitation) cloth always in hand,
occasional closing of the eyes,
and the declaration 'All is <s>Brahman</s>'—
these are the causes of immediate credibility.
Dwelling by a river until midday,
worship of deities in public gatherings,
and constantly wearing clean attire—
this is the life of hypocrisy.
The daily ritual is long
as long as there are spectators present;
everything is abbreviated
as soon as there is no observer.
Tears of bliss and horripilation
obedient to one's own will—
what need has such a person of other spiritual practices?
All kings become his servants.
When punished, they misbehave;
when indulged, all the more so—
for the wicked, therefore, the proper course is
dismissal from a distance.
Non-giving and slight giving
cause some anger in the wicked;
complete giving becomes [their] nature,
and cessation [of giving] becomes the cause of enmity.
Non-association with the wicked is preferable;
association, moreover, [leads] to jealousy;
the arrangement of marriage alliance
is solely for one's own ruin.
Kinship, lack of knowledge,
slander, and poverty—
if these four come together,
then salutations even to that direction!
The heart [set] on others' faults,
the ear on others' affairs,
and speech on others' vulnerabilities—
thus did the Creator fashion the wicked.
Like a scorpion with poison in its tail
[stinging] living beings,
even a tenth part of <s>Kali</s>
makes every age terrible.
Where the wife's words are the <s>Vedas</s>,
where <s>dharma</s> (righteousness) is [merely] a means to wealth,
where one's own cleverness is [the measure of] honor—
salutations to that glorious <s>Kali</s> [age]!
Let the entire world willingly
be subject to this [power of] Time;
for those who have taken refuge in <s>Kālakāla</s> (the Destroyer of Time, i.e., <s>Śiva</s>),
what can Time do to us?
By the poet <s>Nīlakaṇṭha</s>,
this satire of the <s>Kali</s> [age]
was composed for the delight of the learned,
[with] the approval of [the court at] <s>Rājāsthāna</s>.
